🔍Common issues raised in GST dept audit

Background

In the course of audit done by dept under section 65 of the CGST Act, certain issues/objections could be raised. The assesses have to carefully examine the matter, give their explanation.

While it is beingseen that majority of the objections raised at time of audit are not having any legal basis in law, and even if SCN be issued, would be bound to come in favour of assessee in due course at appeals stage.

However in first instance, during course of audit when objections are raised and the submissions done by auditee [could be advised by competent GST professional] with facts, legal grounds[applicable provisions of Act/rules] and supporting circulars/landmark decisions in writing/ to official mail id of concerned officer, it can lead to dropping points at that stage itself, avoidance of issuance of frivolous SCN's, and no ensuing demands with interest penalty and requirement of pre-deposit at appeals stage[10+20%] either.

In this article, the author has examined the common issues being raised at time of audit by department and the validity of the same under the law.

Common issues and its implications

1. Credit availed in GSTR 3B vs 2A/2B
The ITC cannot be denied merely due to the non-reflection of invoices in GSTR-2A/2Bwhen all the conditions specified under Section 16 of CGST Act, 2017 have been satisfied.

GSTR-3B vs GSTR-2A/2B'reconciliation is not required from July 2017 upto 31.12.2021.'No such provision was there in GST law. It was inserted only wef 1.1.2022[ vide inserted section 16(2)(aa)wherein sets out that the invoice details are furnished by supplier in GSTR 1 and be communicated to recipient in 2B.''

The input tax credit is an indefeasible and vested Right. Reliance can be placed in the case of'Shabnam Petrofils Private Limited vs. Union of India (2019) 29 G.S.T.L. 225 (Guj.), Eicher Motors Ltd. Vs UOI - 1999 (106) ELT 3 (SC), Dai Ichi Karkaria vs. UOI - 1999(112) ELT 353(SC).
The facility of GSTR-2A is ONLY for assesses facilitation and credit cannot be denied merely because it is not reflected in GSTR 2A. Refer press release 18th October 2018.

2. Denial of credit due to non payment/short paymentof taxes by vendors

It is near impossible to keep a track of the payment of tax by the supplier/vendor to the government under the existing scheme of returns as the tax is paid in GSTR-3B as the vendor pays the taxes by declaring it in a consolidated manner the principle of Lex Non-Cogit Ad Impossibilia i.e., The law does not compel a man to do that which he cannot possibly perform, as was held in the case of:
Indian Seamless Steel & Alloys Ltd Vs UOI, 2003 (156) ELT 945 (Bom.)

Hico Enterprises Vs CC, 2005 (189) ELT 135 (T-LB). Affirmed by SC in 2008 (228) ELT 161 (SC).
Since the law cannot compel the taxpayers to comply with impossible conditions, whereby auditee does not have access to the portal to check whether supplier has actually paid or not.
Even assuming that the taxes were not paid by vendors on the subject invoices issued, in paperwriter view, the substantial benefit of credit should not be denied due to the default [if any] by vendors. Further, the benefit of the input tax credit cannot be denied to a bona fide purchaser, because of the default of the selling dealer.

Numerous decisions confirm such view in the case of Kay Kay Industries'(2013-TIOL-41-SC-CX). that the manufacturer cannot determine whether his supplier has discharged excise duty on the goods which are supplied to the manufacturer by him.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in the case of'Commissioner of Trade & Taxes, Delhi and others Vs. Arise India Limited'and others [TS-2-SC-2018-VAT]. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi held Section 9(2)(g) of Delhi VAT Act to the extent it disallows Input tax credit(“ITC”) to the purchaser due to default of selling dealer in depositing tax, as violative of Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution of India.

Held D.Y Beathel Enterprises Vs The State tax Officer (Data Cell) [2021-TIOL-890-HC-MAD-GST] if the default is made by non-payment of tax by the seller, the recovery shall be made from the seller.

3. Denial of credit due to cancelled registration of vendors

ITC cannot be denied for the valid transactions.If it is found upon considering the relevant documents that all the purchases and transactions in question are genuine and supported by valid documents and transactions were made before the cancellation of registration of those suppliers than the benefit of input tax credit shall be given to the recipients. Held in LGW Industries'Ltd and Ors vs UOI'[2021-TIOL-2308-HC-KOL-GST]'

4. Denial of credit alleging blocked u/s 17(5)

Air travel/hotel accommodation: The ITC is eligible when nexus is established usage in course of business of auditee, it cannot be denied. Not personal consumption.

CCE vs Fine Care Biosystems (2009 (244) ELT 372 (CESTAT) and Goodluck Steel Tubes Ltd. Vs C. C. Ex., Noida 2013 (32) S.T.R. 123 (Tri. - Del.) ITC on air ticket service charges is eligible when air travel performed for purpose of company business.

Hotel accommodation eligible- One Advertising & Communication Services Ltd. vs C.S.T., Ahmedabad (2012 (27) S.T.R. 344 (Tri. - Ahmd.).

ITC availed on Sales promotion vs gifts: Credit on goods given as gifts is blocked.A 'gift' is commonly defined as a voluntary transfer of property by one to another, without any consideration or compensation therefor.

The Supreme Court cited the definition of 'gift' from Corpus Juris Secundum, Volume 38 in the case of Sonia Bhatia v. State of UP [1981] 2 SCC 585.

When goods such as TV/fridge are given for sales promotion, there is corresponding obligation on the dealers/distributors to lift more goods[more sales and discharge of GST on such outward supplies].

Also when goods are given under schemes such as buy 1 get 1, the value of the so called “freebie” would in normal business course be included in/factored in pricing of the goods being sold[embedded in price], and on which GST is being suffered.

This reasoning is supported in circular 92/11/2019-GST dated 07.03.2019

Consequently, the ITC need not be reversed on business promotion expenses.

Credit related to immoveable property vs moveables or plant and machinery: Section 17(5)(d) restriction is specifically relating to the goods/services used for constructing immovable property, capitalized to immoveable property block meant for self use, and there isno intention of denying credit on the moveable property and plant machinery specifically in Section 17(5). Also there is no restriction to avail credit on the goods/services used for construction of immoveable property but written off to P&L.

The ITC on moveable goods is eligible- such as office equipment could be computers, projectors, stablisers; Electrical fittings such as fan; furniture; furnishings; security systems; fire fighting systems cannot be denied, even if capitalized to immoveable property block as long as supported by valid vendor tax invoices clearly setting out the nature of the inwards supply done to the auditee.

Goods which can be disassembled/dismantled and could be used in other premises without causing any damage to the property, are said to be movable goods. Similarly held in the case of Sirpur Paper Mills'[1998 (97) E.L.T. 3 (S.C.)],'

Similarly credit cannot be denied on plant and machinery, even when it is immoveable. Examples could be credit on HVAC system, Lifts/sewage treatment plant.

Note: Section 3(26) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 defines "Immovable Property" to include land, benefits to arise out of the land, and things attached to the earth, or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth.

Immoveable property means the goods which once fixed to earth cannot be moved/removed without substantial damage.

Personal use/consumption or for official use: Credit is eligible on employee-related expenses, as long as it is incurred in course of discharge of office duties/functions. Examples could be uniforms, ID cards, safety helmets, hand sanitisers, mobile phone for official purpose.

In Steel Authority Of India Ltd vs. CCE (2014 (301) ELT 592 (CESTAT Delhi) credit on shoes used by workers in the Steel plant held eligible

In Indian Rayon & Industries Ltd.vs. Commr of C. Ex., Bhavnagar (2006 (4) S.T.R. 79 (Tri. - Mumbai) held that the tax paid on mobile phone is available as credit to eligible service providers of output service and manufacturers in absence of any express prohibition under CCR.

On a related note, ITC is eligible on canteen facility even though consumed by person, when it is mandatory for employer to provide facility under law for time being in force[vide amendment made wef February 2019]. Example canteen facility provided under Factories Act is eligible credit and cannot be denied citing personal consumption.

5. Non payment of Reverse charge liability under section 9(3) r/w notification 13/2017-CT(R); Section 9(4)

RCM on GTO vs GTA: When the transporter of goods by road service issues a consignment note/LR then it would be covered as GTA service. Tax liability to be paid by registered recipient.' Credit can be availed to extent used to make taxable supplies.

When consignment note is not issued, can consider not as GTA but GTO, GST exemption is there, and not liable to pay tax under RCM.
Post 18.7.2022:' GST need not be paid under RCM on GTA service when the vendor has opted to discharge tax liability under forward charge[FCM].

RCM on import of services: All payments made to foreign vendors towards services supplied to Indian recipient entity are not liable to tax as import of services under reverse charge. First need to determine what is place of supply[POS], within or outside India vide section 13(2) to (13) of IGST Act.

Few examples could be: Place of supply of training done in physical presence outside India, accommodation/food consumed outside, travel done outside India, services performed physically on goods outside India, transport of goods destination outside India, Trade event/exhibition in Germany- All instances where POS outside India-no RCM.

RCM on holding share capitalin Indian subsidiary as supply of service:This is a frivolous objection being raised. There cannot be levy of GST on investment in securities which'is'neither good nor service. Hence, it cannot be treated as a supply under any provision of the GST Act including under Section 7(1)(c)-import of services from related persons, and as a result, the levy itself fails.

RCM on director remuneration: GST is not leviable when the director is employee and paid remuneration as services by employee to employer in course of employment covered in Entry 1 Schedule III neither supply of goods nor services. Circular 140/10/2020 - GSTcan be referred.

Company not liable to pay tax under RCM on rent paid to Directors in their Individual Capacity.Cords Cable Industries Limited Vs Commissioner, Central Excise (CESTAT Delhi). Appeal Number : Service Tax Appeal No. 52207 of 2018 ST case.

RCM on development rights: Can be contended that it is benefit fromland, which is covered in Schedule III Entry 5 sale of land which is neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services. Consequently not taxable to GST. Dept may dispute as there is no exemption given in GST nor any judicial precedents in GST law in this regard as of date.

Note RCM on the DR was introduced only in respect of JDA entered post 1.4.2019, not prior to that dateand for earlier periods JDA's, RCM liability cannot be applied on promoter/Developer at all.

RCM being demanded on security services/renting of motor vehicle: GST under RCM was made applicable on the security services done by person[other than body corporate] to registered person wef 1.1.2019. Not taxable for period prior to that date.

Similarly for renting of motor vehicle done by person[other than body corporate] and not discharging tax at 12% where recipient is the body corporate, tax to be paid under RCM wef 1.1.2020. For period from 1.10.2019 till 31.1.22019 renting of motor vehicle done [other than by body corporate] and paying GST at 5% with ITC only in same line of business to recipient being body corporate was liable in hands of receiver under RCM.

Note: Prior to those dates of introduction of the levy u/s 9(3), no GST under RCM can be demanded for the above services.

Non payment of Reverse charge liability u/s 9(4) in respect of procurements done from unregistered suppliers: The levy was only for period of July 2017 till Oct 12th 2017. Thereafter in abeyance and then only for real estate developers post April 2019 onwards. View could be no intention of Govt to levy at all-has to be judicially tested.

Exemption when procurements not exceeding Rs.5000 per day[vide notification 8/2017-CT(R). When exceeding such limit, GST to be paid on procurements from unregistered persons towards taxable supplies.

Note: Even if GST were to be paid under RCM on procurements of specified services from unregistered suppliers[such as import of consulting services from abroad ]/unregistered supplier procurements on which there was valid liability, and such tax voluntarily paid now[even if paid during course of audit] ITC can be availed[even for past years of July 2017 onwards under self invoice of current date].

6. Demand of GST on deposits received'

Mere receipt of refundable deposits/deposits received, which are clearly disclosed under current liabilities cannot be alleged to be taxable to GST. Deposit is not taxable to GST until applied towards taxable supplies of goods/services by the supplier.[Refer proviso to definition of consideration Section 2(31)].

7. Short declared turnovers in 3B vs GSTR 9/3B vs sales register/GSTR 3B vs 1

Reasons for difference to be provided along with reconciliation statement to establish correctness of taxes paid.

8. Mismatch of GST paid under reverse charge and credit availed

Reasons for difference to be provided along with reconciliation statement of taxes paid and credit being availed.

9. Notice period Recovery/compensation for business loss/short lifted material /forfeited amounts due to cancelled service

There is no corresponding supply of goods/services in these cases levy fails. Circular 178/2022 has clarified on non taxability-circular binding on dept officers Dhiren Chemicals [2002 (143) ELT 19 (SC)]

10. Exports of service paid for in CFE treated as taxable to GST alleging POS is India
Agreement/SOWs would be paramount to establish nature of services. Proof of deliverables such as reports/emails submitted to foreign clients. This is more seen in alleging outsourced support services[POS as per section 13(2) location of foreign recipient client] to be intermediary services[taxable as POS vide section 13(8) of IGST Act is location of Indian supplier].

Plethora of favourable decisions are there in erstwhile ST laws and thereafter as well to support auditee. In Ohmi Industries Asia Pvt. Ltd. vs. Assistant Commissioner '[TS-128-HC(DEL)-2023-GST] HC: held assessee not 'intermediary' for provision of services to Japanese affiliate, allows IGST refund.

Conclusion

Where the stakes are high, the assessee is also suggested to consult with expert professionals in indirect taxes and GST, and based on their opinion, take a call to contest orpay voluntarily[wherever valid liability is there].

In order to avoid any surprises during audit, it is also suggested to get pre-audit done internally / externally by competent professional CA's. During pre-audit if any valid tax liability omitted/ unpaid found out [such as RCM on import of services/GTA services], discharge voluntarily with interest[to avoid penalty- if found in course of dept audit].

In this article the paper writer has given practical issues and the replies which if properly drafted could certainly help to avoid/reduce frivolous objections and relief by way of dropping of demands at the stage of audit itself[prior to SCN].

These actions often happen under two parallel mechanisms of India’s Information Technology Act, 2000.

Section 69A allows the Government to issue blocking orders on broad grounds such as national security or public order. However, these orders are usually confidential, and affected users often receive neither notice nor a copy of the blocking order, making it difficult to challenge them.

Separately, Section 79(3)(b) allows authorities to pressure platforms to remove content by threatening loss of “safe harbour” protections if platforms fail to comply with government or court directions. In practice, this creates strong incentives for platforms to over-comply.

The lack of transparency around these processes raises serious concerns for due process, free expression, and accountability.

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

Can the Government suspend a political party’s Instagram handle without a clear statutory power? And can a politician boycott a courtroom while simultaneously asking the Supreme Court to transfer the same judge from hearing his case?  

This week, the Aam Aadmi Party raised both questions in two different constitutional courtrooms.  

In the Supreme Court, AAP challenged the suspension of its Gujarat unit’s Instagram handle, arguing that Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act was never meant to become a direct content-blocking weapon. 

Senior Advocate Shadan Farasat argued that the provision only deals with “safe harbour” obligations of intermediaries — not independent censorship powers.  The party says the move violates Article 19(1)(a), the constitutional guarantee of free speech. 

The Supreme Court has now issued notice to the Centre.  At the same time in the Delhi High Court, Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma appointed three amicus curiae for Arvind Kejriwal, Manish Sisodia, and Satyendar Jain after the leaders chose to boycott proceedings, invoking “Mahatma Gandhi’s Satyagraha principles” and claiming their faith in the court process had been shaken.  

But here’s the constitutional twist: Kejriwal had also moved the Supreme Court seeking transfer of the excise policy case away from Justice Sharma’s bench — even as his legal team withdrew from participation before her court.  

This has now created a rare constitutional confrontation involving: 
⚖️ Article 19 vs state regulation of digital speech 
⚖️ Article 21 vs procedural fairness in criminal prosecution 
⚖️ Judicial recusal vs courtroom boycott 
⚖️ Free speech, due process, and strategic constitutional litigation  Justice Sharma’s response may become one of the most significant procedural moments in the case: instead of proceeding ex parte, she chose to appoint independent senior advocates as amicus curiae to preserve procedural fairness.  

And one line from the Supreme Court hearing may define this entire battle: “Today my portal is gone.”  Because this is no longer just about an Instagram account.

 It is about whether opposition parties in India can lose their digital voice overnight — and what constitutional remedy exists when that happens.

Loops vs. Graphs, clearly explained!

loops are great, but they have a ceiling:

a loop makes one unit of work better. it cannot decide which units exist.

so you end up with a very good agent running the wrong three steps, in the wrong order, one at a time.

Graph engineering fixes this by moving the decision up a layer: what runs, what runs at the same time, and what never runs at all.

you need both. here's how it works:

a graph splits your system into two kinds of decision.

↳ inside a unit: the loop. produce, check, correct, repeat until green
↳ between units: the graph. split, fan out, merge, gate, send back

Prompts → Context → Harness → Loops → Graphs

you get parallel work, isolated contexts, and steps that stop running when nothing needs them.

the trick is being selective about what becomes a node.

only spend a model where judgment lives. merging, ranking, deduping and schema checks are edges, and edges are code. 

free, instant, and they cannot be argued out of a verdict. a graph where every edge is an agent pays rent on its own wiring.

one thing to know before you scale it.

a graph has two return paths, and almost everyone builds one.

↳ the correction edge is short. a gate rejects one unit back to the step that produced it, and it fixes the run you are in
↳ the learning edge is long. an accepted result goes back to the splitter as a constraint, and it fixes every run after

skip the second and you get a graph that is fast and never gets smarter. next week it starts from the same place with the same blind spots.

and a smaller one that eats whole nights: when a unit fails, return that unit, not the batch. 

send back four slices because one failed and you have just rewritten three correct ones. do it twice in a run and the run never converges.

Alright, since the Dunning-Kruger Awards this week are going to people who apparently cannot tell the difference between one tragic murder case and an entire population, if we’re gonna go there, let’s go there.

I got these statistics from Grok regarding postpartum issues and murder rates. Feel free to fact-check.

I asked Grok:

What percent of American men commit murder?
• Roughly 0.3–0.7%. That’s 3 to 7 out of every thousand men, or around 1 in 150–300.

What percent of American women commit murder?
• Roughly 0.04–0.1%. That’s 4 to 10 out of every ten thousand women, or around 1 in 1,000–2,500.

Women account for only about 10–12% of known murder offenders. Men make up the rest.

In contrast, the lifetime murder victimization rate is 0.68% for males and 0.19% for females. Compare these to the numbers above. While men are at higher odds of being murdered, men’s average population risks of murdering versus being murdered are similar. Women, however, are at much greater risk of being murdered than of committing murder.

Now let’s look at postpartum moms.

10–15% of mothers will experience postpartum depression (PPD). Only 0.1–0.2% of mothers will experience postpartum psychosis (PPP). PPD is 50 to 100 times more common than PPP.

The total rate of filicide by postpartum women is extremely rare—on the order of a few cases per 100,000 (well under 0.01%, and typically estimated in the range of roughly 2–8 per 100,000 live births for maternal involvement in infant homicide, depending on the exact definition and data source).

Postpartum psychosis (distinct from the more common postpartum depression or “baby blues”) occurs in roughly 1–2 per 1,000 births. Older estimates sometimes cited an ~4% risk of infanticide among untreated cases, but this figure has been questioned as potentially overstated based on misreadings of follow-up studies. The absolute contribution to overall numbers remains tiny.

How do these numbers compare?

The number of postpartum women who commit filicide is much smaller than the number of women who commit any kind of murder, which is itself much smaller than the number of men who commit murder.

10–15% of mothers will experience postpartum depression.

Only 0.1–0.2% of women will experience postpartum psychosis specifically (1–2 out of every 1,000 births). This is lower than the percentage of men who murder (3 to 7 out of every 1,000 men).

Read that again. Postpartum psychosis—without even factoring in murder—is less common than men who murder.

Of those with untreated postpartum psychosis, as many as 4 out of every 100 may commit murder, but those numbers are in question and may be lower. Since postpartum psychosis is itself rate, we are looking at up to four percent of 0.1–0.2% is 0.004%, or four out of every hundred thousand. The smallest number we've seen here.

So: out of every hundred thousand births, up to four may result in a postpartum-psychosis-related murder. This is roughly on par with the number of men who kill their own children — a few per hundred thousand. Meanwhile, the number of men who murder anyone is about 75 to 175 times higher than the number of women who kill their children.

If people are going to get hysterical about this issue—senselessly equating postpartum women with postpartum depression, postpartum depression with postpartum psychosis, and postpartum psychosis with murder—then by the same logic we should equate men in general with murder, because the percent of men who murder is higher than the percent of women with any of these issues.

Thankfully, I’m afflicted by no such hysteria. I’m happily married, get along well with many good men, and can tell the difference between a normal, decent man and an internet troll with no greater purpose in life than harassing women online between porn sessions. Grow up and get a life, fellas.

It’s safe to say that the world changed a lot in the last five years. It certainly did for me. After putting out Total Freedom in 2020 then accepting the fact that touring it and promoting it wasn’t going to happen, I went back to my coffee shop and worked, I got married, I moved (twice), and I even found myself living in a new country.

When the summer of 2022 rolled in, I was able to make up for lost time on the road until 2023 when I was ready to head to St. Petersburg, Florida and take some well-earned time to write. It was in early 2024 after sending him my cover version of his song “Traveling Alone” that Jason Isbell and I first talked about working together, and incredibly he offered to produce these songs, enlisting Gena Johnson as co-producer. 

Pinch me.

Fast forward to September 2024 - Jason, Gena and I started making this album at Sound Emporium in Nashville. Jason enlisted members of the 400 Unit to be our rhythm section. We recorded the songs that eventually became the 10 tracks on “Billionaire”. I am so indebted and thankful to Jason and Gena for their dedication, their time, their care and their talents - in championing me and my work, and to all the musicians who appear on this album coming out August 22nd. 

It’s true when they say your songs are like your children and you can’t pick favorites (not out loud, at least).  But I love the two we’re putting out today.  “Save Your Soul” and “Say Goodbye, Tell No One” kick off this album sonically the way I had hoped my new record would sound - tough and cool, vulnerable and honest.

My favorite songwriters and bands are written all over my work, for which I am unapologetic.  Songs that tell the story of looking through the rear view mirror on my way to something new, watching a version of myself and my life behind me get smaller on the horizon as I go. I found the last five years fraught with challenges of all kinds, highs and lows, profound grief, grit and determination, anger and even unabashed joy in my new locale (and very tanned legs). 

Thanks for listening and staying tuned for all the ones that will be released in the coming weeks.  For the foreseeable future, I will be touring with my band, an exceptional group of musicians who are my best friends and we plan on burning down the fucking house every night thank you very much.  

Here we go.

So swing by and stream the songs, check out the show calendar, pre-order some vinyl and check out some of the goodies we’ve put together for you.

THANK YOU.

Apparently Experience Is Terrifying Now!

Think of this as a small thought experiment in what Canadians say they want in a Prime Minister versus whom they actually choose

There is something about Pierre Poilievre that drives a particular kind of Canadian absolutely insane. Not disagreement. No, THAT would be normal. I mean the visceral stuff.

Things like the instant sneer or label of "Skippy" at the mere mention of his name. Or the "Career politician" sputtered in contemptible disgust by so many without a clue of why this even upsets them in the first place, but they heard it on the CBC so it must be true.  "Never had a real job" is shouted by the other half of the ignorant class who have never lifted a finger to fact check the claim for themselves. You know, the sort of reaction normally reserved for discovering someone microwaved fish in the staff lunchroom.

And I've been trying to understand it because, frankly, the logic is bizarre. Strip away the names, remove the party colours, and forget who CBC told you was scary this week and pretend you're hiring somebody to manage an actual organization instead. 

Two resumes land on your kitchen table. One candidate grew up in a middle-class household, was adopted by two schoolteachers, attended ordinary public school, earned a university degree in international relations and has spent more than two decades learning and practicing within the institution he's applying to lead.

He was elected to Parliament at 25. He’s served in government and opposition, held cabinet portfolios, introduced Bill C-23 The Fair Elections Act and received royal assent, he studied parliamentary procedure, worked on economic files and spent years being questioned, challenged and publicly accountable for his positions.

You can hate every policy he's ever proposed, that's fine, but nobody can seriously claim the guy accidentally strolled into Parliament looking for directions.

Then there's the other résume. This candidate spent much of his adult professional life among some of the world's most powerful financial institutions... Goldman Sachs, the Bank of Canada, the Bank of England, Brookfield, most of it outside the country he was born in.

His natural habitat includes international boards, global finance, Davos-level circles, and lavish rooms where nobody has ever stared at their debit card wondering whether the grocery store is going to approve $187.43.

He's extremely accomplished, and that's not sarcasm. Mark Carney has an impressive résume. It's simply an impressive résume from a completely different universe than the one most Canadians actually live in. And before him, Liberals chose Justin Trudeau, the son of a former prime minister, raised with extraordinary privilege, political access and a last name that came with its own voter recognition.

So explain this one to me:  why is the guy raised by schoolteachers the dangerous "elite," while actual elites keep getting marketed as champions of ordinary Canadians?

This isn't even really about Poilievre. It's about the Liberal Party's favourite little parlour trick: if somebody becomes politically dangerous, don't beat the argument. Brand the person until low-information voters are either afraid to examine the argument themselves or are successfully gaslit into blind acceptance.

They toss labels like "extremist," or "far-right," and "dangerous." Then they cycle through the next set and use labels like "angry," "Populist," and "purveyors of misinformation," or whatever adjective survived the morning focus group.

Repeat it often enough, have enough friendly media voices repeat it too, and apparently we're supposed to mistake character assassination for evidence. It's incredibly efficient. Why defend your record when you can simply convince people that anyone pointing at it is unhinged? THAT'S the part that deserves contempt!

They don't need you to prove Poilievre wrong. They just need you sufficiently conditioned to hate him that you'll never bother checking whether he's right. Somewhere along the way, "career politician" became a devastating insult while "career international financier who had never held elected office" became reassuring evidence of competence.

Think about how stupid that is.🤦🏼‍♀️ If your furnace quits in Saskatchewan in January, nobody says:  "Absolutely not. Don't call the guy who's repaired furnaces for twenty years. He's a CAREER furnace technician."

Nobody recoils from the mechanic with 25 years of experience. And nobody demands a surgeon who has never performed surgery because the experienced guy has been doing it suspiciously long and might very well be a dreaded expert.  

Apparently experience becomes a character defect only when we're choosing the people running the country.
Instead, we'd apparently prefer somebody who has never touched a furnace a day in his life, but has delivered several internationally acclaimed lectures on the future of furnace heat.

You can't convince me that logic makes perfect sense. And then there's the whole "relatable" thing. This may be my favourite part.

Poilievre gets mocked for being ambitious, rehearsed and political. Well... yes, d'uh. He's a politician. If "Being A Politician 101" were a University course, these traits and skills would be the course material. The logic employed here absolutely escapes me. This is rather like discovering your dentist has developed a fascination with teeth.

Meanwhile Canadians spent years being told Trudeau understood ordinary families while ordinary families increasingly couldn't afford ordinary houses. Now we're told Carney understands workers because he understands economies. Those are not even remotely the same thing.

A person can understand inflation beautifully on a spreadsheet without knowing what it feels like when hamburger finally goes on sale and you still can’t afford to buy any. That doesn't make wealthy people bad and it doesn't make bankers evil. And nobody needs to have driven a forklift before becoming Prime Minister.

But lived distance from ordinary life matters when you're making decisions that alter ordinary life for everybody else.

👉🏻 A carbon policy looks different from the back seat of a limousine than it does from a pickup truck that has to travel 70 kilometres for groceries.
👉🏻 An electricity regulation looks different in a boardroom than it does on the factory floor or when the bill lands on the kitchen table.
👉🏻 A housing policy sounds considerably different when you've never wondered whether your kid will ever afford one.

That’s not class warfare, that, everyone, is perspective. 

And the Liberal definition of “elite” has become almost performance art. A man raised by schoolteachers who entered Parliament young and spent his adult life in Canadian public service is dismissed as an out-of-touch career politician.

Meanwhile, a multimillionaire international financier who spent most of his working adult years working outside the country in London, New York and global financial circles arrives and somehow becomes the natural voice of ordinary, every day Canadians.

You really have to admire the marketing. If Kellogg's could convince Canadians Frosted Flakes were a leafy green superfood, we'd nominate their communications department for an Order of Canada.

And no, none of this means Poilievre must therefore be a wonderful Prime Minister. Maybe you dislike him, or maybe you despise his policies. Perhaps hearing him speak causes your left eyelid to twitch. Have at it then. But instead of becoming unhinged the moment somebody says "Pierre," criticize the actual policies.

Tell us which economic proposal is wrong. Tell us which tax proposal fails and why. Tell us which housing proposal won’t work while you’re at it. And please, enlighten the rest of us as to which foreign-policy position is terrifying when Poilievre proposes it but suddenly becomes sensible statesmanship when Carney steals the idea and does it himself. That right there ought to be thoroughly entertaining.

Explain Pierre Poilievre Derangement Syndrome to us all and it's underlying trigger that seems borne of hypocrisy. Because "Skippy" isn't an argument. It's what you say when you've run out of one. And once the personalities, photographs and party logos disappear, we're left with something considerably more uncomfortable.

So let's try something.

The image below shows two Canadian political leaders with the names, photos, parties and tribal decorations removed.
Try this on a Liberal voter in your life before showing them the answer. 😂

Read both profiles. No Googling. Pick who seems better qualified to lead Canada, then decide which is #PierrePoilievre and which is #MarkCarney.

Don’t study it to death. If you stare long enough, the answer becomes obvious. The point is who you thought they were before it did. 

Those politically informed will have no trouble with this.

A YEAR AGO, THE SUPREME COURT SAID: “THE VOTER MUST KNOW.”

But in Uttarakhand, some voters reportedly say they found out about objections against their names from journalists — not from the election authorities.

The bigger story is about something more fundamental: rules, transparency and accountability in the voter-list revision process.

The script raises serious questions over how ECI’s limits on bulk objections were changed, whether safeguards were properly communicated, and whether the Supreme Court’s earlier directions were actually implemented on the ground.

And then comes the uncomfortable question:

If a Supreme Court order says a voter must be informed when their name is deleted — who checks whether that order was actually followed?

Because an order is only as strong as its implementation.

And when election rolls determine who gets to vote, transparency isn’t a technical detail.

It is the foundation of trust in the election itself.

What do you think — should the Supreme Court demand a compliance report on its own election-related orders?

9 Critical Nuclear Energy Stories for Policy and Defense Leaders

Stay ahead of the rapidly shifting nuclear landscape with Press Monitor's curated press review. According to Press Monitor's tracking of Indian publications, today's print media brings you the most critical developments in nuclear energy, weapons, and trade — from India's SHANTI Act liability framework to escalating global tensions. This media intelligence roundup covers the stories that matter for decision-makers. Here are 9 essential updates you need to know, sourced from national dailies across India.

1. SHANTI Act Liability Caps Finalised
A front-page report in Indian Express says the Department of Atomic Energy has released draft rules for the SHANTI Act, which establish graded liability caps reviewed every five years by an expert group. The new framework sets maximum liability for nuclear operators between Rs 100 crore and Rs 3000 crore based on reactor size, replacing the previous general cap of Rs 1500 crore. The rules also address concerns regarding the operator's right of recourse against nuclear equipment suppliers.
Why it matters: India's nuclear liability regime is foundational for private sector participation and international reactor supply.
Key detail: The Department of Atomic Energy released draft rules under the SHANTI Act, setting graded liability caps from Rs 100 crore to Rs 3,000 crore based on reactor size. Caps will be reviewed every five years by an expert group. Operators retain right of recourse against equipment suppliers.

Source: Front-page report by Pratyush Deep, Indian Express.
Next step: Industry stakeholders should submit comments before final rules are gazetted.
Question: Is the graded cap sufficient to attract global reactor vendors?

2. Trump Threatens Iran with Economic Warfare
US President Donald Trump insisted on policies he described as failed would bring further failures and alienate Iranians. He said America’s economic terrorism threatens the global economy and the national sovereignty of countries around the world. Trump has yet to achieve the objectives he set out at the start of the war: dismantling Iran’s nuclear programme, curbing its ability to attack regional rivals, and creating conditions for Iranians to overthrow their clerical rulers. Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates suspended all trade activities with Iran, Oman is negotiating an agreement on managing the Strait of Hormuz, and Trump threatened to bomb Oman if it ‘gets in the way.’
Why it matters: US-Iran tensions directly impact global oil prices, nuclear proliferation risk, and trade routes.
Key detail: President Trump warned of unprecedented economic consequences for nations supporting Iran. Iran's foreign minister condemned the move as economic terrorism. UAE suspended trade with Iran; Oman negotiated Hormuz management.

Source: Business Line, Delhi edition.
Next step: Monitor Indian crude imports and remittance routes through the Gulf.
Question: How will India balance energy needs with diplomatic pressure?

3. Pakistan Passes Military and Nuclear Command Bills
A front-page report in New Indian Express says Pakistan’s National Assembly passed two bills related to the military and nuclear command structure. The Defence Forces of Pakistan Act, 2O26 and the amended National Command Authority Act, 2OlO were presented by Defence Minister Khawaja Asif while Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif was present in the lower house of parliament.
Why it matters: Legal changes to Pakistan's nuclear command structure affect regional stability and non-proliferation.
Key detail: The National Assembly passed the Defence Forces of Pakistan Act, 2026 and an amendment to the National Command Authority Act, 2010. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif presented both bills with PM Shehbaz Sharif present.

Source: Front-page, New Indian Express, Chennai edition.
Next step: Track Pakistan's nuclear doctrine disclosures under the amended acts.
Question: Does this enhance or undermine civilian oversight of nuclear assets?

4. North Korea Launches 10 Ballistic Missiles
A front-page report in Asian Age says South Korea’s presidential office condemned the launch of more than 10 short-range ballistic missiles on Thursday and ordered its military to maintain full readiness during ongoing joint exercises with the United States. The launch came after North Korea’s Kim Yo Jong condemned the US-South Korea military drills.
Why it matters: Missile tests during US-South Korea joint drills heighten Northeast Asia security risks.
Key detail: Over 10 short-range ballistic missiles launched Thursday; South Korea condemned the provocation. Kim Yo Jong criticised the joint exercises.

Source: Asian Age, Delhi edition.
Next step: Review India's missile defense preparedness and diplomatic posture.
Question: Is North Korea's testing cycle tied to US election timelines?

5. Nuclear Capacity vs. Electricity Bills — Cost Challenge
A front-page report in Mint says India has set a goal of reaching 100GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047 but the tariffs from these plants may not be competitive against cheaper renewable energy options.
Why it matters: India's 100 GW nuclear target by 2047 faces economic viability questions.
Key detail: Mint reports tariffs from new nuclear plants may not compete with cheap renewable energy. Cost overruns and long construction timelines remain hurdles.

Source: Front-page, Mint, by Alok Kumar.
Next step: Compare levelised cost of nuclear vs solar+storage in upcoming NITI Aayog reports.
Question: Can small modular reactors (SMRs) change the cost equation?

6. China Rejects Sanctions on Iran, Calls for Diplomacy
A front-page report in Financial Express says, China calls on relevant parties to take responsible measures and sought to solve the issue through diplomatic and political means.
Why it matters: Chinese position influences global sanctions regime and oil markets.
Key detail: Beijing urged responsible parties to solve the Iran issue through diplomatic and political means, opposing unilateral sanctions.

Source: Financial Express, Delhi edition.
Next step: Analyse Indian diplomatic alignment between Quad partners and Iran trade.
Question: Will China's stance give Iran economic breathing room?

7. India Removes Pakistan High Commission Queue Liners
"Selon The Times of India, Indian authorities removed queue liners outside the Pakistan high commission visa section along with other encroachment on a lane outside the compound. The action Wednesday followed removal of parking poles and security barricades outside the Indian high commission in Islamabad earlier this week. Official sources said the liners were removed from a side lane outside the high commission and not the main gate. The response was said to be proportionate to the Pakistaniaction outside the Indian mission. Official sources said India was hoping the matter would end here but added govt would respond accordingly if Pakistan chooses to escalate. India’s ties with Pakis-tan remain in a freeze with govt last year after the Pahalgam terror attack cutting down the strength of high commissions from the already downgraded 55 to 3O. Both sides continue to have functional engagements though, including DGMO-level talks, exchange of pre-notification of flight testing of ballistic missiles, exchange of list of nuclear installations, and exchange of list of prisoners in each other's custody. India strongly denies having any Track-2 dialogue with Pakistan. Visuals showed that India’s action left a trail of rubble outside the mission, with broken metal railings and gates, twisted metal frames, roofing sheets, bricks and chunks of concrete and plaster strewn across the paved area. The main entrance of the high commission, with its white walls, domed features and large metal gates bear the Pakistani emblem, remained intact,"
Why it matters: Tit-for-tat diplomatic actions impact nuclear confidence-building measures and consular access.
Key detail: Indian authorities removed queue liners and security barricades outside Pakistan High Commission in Delhi. Action followed similar removal at Indian mission in Islamabad. Both sides continue nuclear and ballistic missile pre-notification exchanges.

Source: Times of India, New Delhi edition.
Next step: Monitor impact on bilateral nuclear confidence-building measures.
Question: Could this escalate to disrupt consular prisoner exchanges?

8. World Beyond the Shadow of Nuclear Explosions
A front-page report in State Times says that since the first nuclear test in 1945, more than two thousand nuclear explosions have been conducted across the world, leaving behind environmental destruction, human suffering, displacement, and long-lasting radioactive contamination.
Why it matters: Environmental and humanitarian costs of 2,000+ nuclear tests call for renewed disarmament efforts.
Key detail: Since 1945, over 2,000 nuclear detonations have caused radioactive contamination, displacement, and health crises. Article ahead of International Day Against Nuclear Tests.

Source: State Times, Jammu edition, by Gourav Sabharwal and Kashish Sabharwal.
Next step: Advocate for ratification of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) by holdout states.
Question: Can India push for a global test ban while maintaining credible deterrence?

9. Trump Narrowly Focused as Midterms Approach
A front-page report in Hindustan Times says President Donald Trump remains fixated on a narrow set of concerns, including building monuments to his own greatness, clamping down on immigration, and pressuring to make voting harder for American citizens. Despite these actions, he may escape political repercussions due to gerrymandering and lack of a unified Democratic message.
Why it matters: Presidential priorities shape US foreign policy, including nuclear deals with Iran and arms control.
Key detail: Trump remains fixated on immigration, monuments, and the SAVE Act, while ignoring public concerns on inflation — compounding the Iran war's economic impact. He may escape electoral punishment due to gerrymandering.

Source: Hindustan Times, Delhi edition.
Next step: Assess how US domestic politics will affect Iran nuclear negotiations and arms control talks.
Question: Will a change in Congress alter US nuclear posture?

The Silent Emergency: Eleven Years Under the Shadow of Control

India, the land of a billion vibrant voices, is grappling with a chilling silence. For eleven years under the PM, we've witnessed an

"Undeclared Emergency@11"

—no declared curfews, no tanks, but a steady erosion of our democratic freedoms. This is the story of a Nation fighting for its soul, where the cost of speaking out grows heavier daily.

The Press in Chains
Our Fourth Estate, once a beacon of truth, now falters under relentless pressure. V-Dem and Freedom House 2025 reports label India an “electoral autocracy,” ranked “partly free.” The Press Freedom Index places us at 159/176, near Somalia’s shadow. Honest journalists face arrests, raids, and intimidation for daring to question. Laws like UAPA and sedition are weaponized, branding critics “terrorists” without trial. Media houses face raids, their voices stifled. Modi’s 11-year tenure without a single press conference speaks volumes—hate speech thrives, but truth is jailed.

Homes Turned to Rubble
Bulldozers roar across India, not for progress but as tools of vengeance. Homes, often of minorities or dissenters, are demolished in displays of state power. Families stand amid rubble, targeted for their identity or beliefs. Ministers spewing hate are rewarded, while citizens live in fear. This isn’t the India we fought for.

The Digital Gag
In the age of X, FB, Insta, and YouTube, where voices once soared, dissent is now caged. Content creators and tweeters face arrests for “misinformation” or “inciting unrest.” Over 20,000 independent voices have been silenced, their crime often a post challenging the regime. This is a democracy where keyboards are as dangerous as megaphones.

Opposition Under Siege
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has become a weapon to intimidate opposition leaders, with raids targeting those who refuse to bow to the BJP. Homes and offices of opposition figures are stormed, cases piled up to coerce them into joining the ruling party or face relentless harassment. This blatant misuse of agencies undermines democracy, turning dissent into a dangerous act.

Puppet Election Commission
The Election Commission, once a pillar of democratic integrity, now dances to the tune of the BJP. The removal of the Chief Justice of India from the selection committee for appointing Election Commissioners has raised alarms about its independence. This move, critics argue, ensures a pliable EC, ready to tilt the electoral scales. Free and fair elections, the heartbeat of democracy, now pulse under the shadow of control.

The Leader’s Shadow
Modi’s image dominates—billboards, screens, even vaccine certificates and rail tickets. Supporters call it leadership; we see a cult stifling dissent. Parliament weakened, constitutional bodies eroded, divisive figures glorified—this is a five-fold assault on our democracy. BJP invokes 1975’s Emergency to deflect, but today’s control needs no formal name. It’s a slow, silent strangulation of our freedoms.

Nation’s Resolve
Fifty years ago, India resisted the 1975 Emergency. Today, the shackles are subtler but real. Jailed journalists, bulldozed homes, silenced voices, ED raids on opposition leaders, and a compromised Election Commission tell of a democracy under siege. As Modi marks “Samvidhan Hatya Diwas,” we say the real threat to our Constitution is now—unnamed, insidious, but ever-present.

India stands at a crossroads. Will we reclaim our chorus of voices or let silence prevail? The fight for our democracy lies in the courage of those who speak, write, and dream of a free tomorrow. 

#UndeclaredEmergency #SaveDemocracy

Starlink is no longer just expanding It is steadily surrounding India. 🇮🇳

It is already operational in Bhutan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, while Nepal is also moving towards adoption. Every neighbour India has except China is either on Starlink or getting there.

Now connect the dots.

Over the past few years governments changed in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Nepal.

Each time, Starlink was not just embedded but actively used to keep protest movements connected when those governments tried to shut the internet down.

We have seen in Iran exactly how US-controlled satellite internet becomes an operational tool the moment a government tries to cut its own network.

Starlink bypasses ground infrastructure entirely, No government can filter, monitor or cut it through conventional means once it is being used.

China looked at this exact scenario and banned Starlink entirely and It built its own satellite internet through the Thousand Sails constellation instead. 

India currently holds Starlink at the licensing stage and has not yet allowed full commercial rollout.

Pausing is the right instinct but it is not a permanent answer. India needs to decide now, before the rollout begins, whether it wants a US-controlled satellite network operating on its soil or whether it takes China's approach and shuts the door completely.

The Centre has issued a notice to messaging platform Telegram, directing it to take concrete measures within 15 days to curb the widespread circulation of pirated films, OTT content and other copyrighted audio-visual material on its platform.

The notice, issued by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (I&B) on July 4, asks Telegram to strengthen its mechanisms for detecting, reporting, disabling access to and removing infringing content. The move is aimed at safeguarding India's creator economy, film industry, broadcasters, OTT platforms, producers and distributors.

The government has also instructed the platform to take action against repeat offenders, including channels, groups, bots, accounts, administrators and associated entities involved in the dissemination of pirated content.

In addition, Telegram has been asked to furnish details of its grievance redressal mechanism available to producers, OTT platforms and law-enforcement agencies, and to submit an Action Taken Report within 15 days outlining the measures implemented to prevent and remove piracy-related material.

The notice signals a shift towards greater platform accountability rather than relying solely on individual takedown requests. The government has previously acted against more than 3,000 Telegram channels allegedly carrying pirated content.

The development comes amid increasing scrutiny of digital platforms over content regulation and compliance. Telegram was also temporarily blocked in India until June 22 in connection with concerns surrounding the NEET-UG re-examination process following allegations of a paper leak and a subsequent investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

How Modi Managed “THE MEDIA” To Stay In Power

In 2002, Gujarat CM Narendra Modi sat in front of a BBC camera and admitted his one real weakness:
“One area where I was very, very weak… that was how to handle the media.”

He never forgot that lesson. He just decided the media should never be allowed to become a problem again.
Fast forward to 2026.
Between March and July, the government sent one blocking order every 68 seconds to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube.

1.95 lakh orders in five months.
1,275 every single day.
Instagram — the platform students used during the Jantar Mantar protests — received more than 1 lakh of them.
Last year the daily average was six.

This is not “managing” the media.
This is industrial-scale silencing.

The same playbook that started with ED and CBI cases against NDTV, the takeover of Network18, and UAPA against NewsClick’s founder is now running on autopilot through the Sahyog portal. Content vanishes in three hours. Often without anyone even seeing the order.

A government that needs to issue a takedown every 68 seconds is not confident.
It is terrified of what people will say when they are not being watched.

That is how you stay in power for this long — not by answering questions, but by making sure the questions never reach the public.

When dissent is treated as a security threat and protest as a crime, the media is no longer a watchdog. It is just another department to be controlled.
The 2002 admission was honest.

The 2026 response is the real story. 68 seconds.
That’s how long this government takes to silence you.
He admitted one weakness in 2002. He spent the next 24 years making sure it never happened again.
