9 Critical SMB & SME Stories for Entrepreneurs

Stay ahead with today's top media monitoring insights on Indian SMBs and SMEs. From Delhi's mega MSME capacity drive to NITI Aayog's early skilling push, here are the stories shaping the ecosystem. This press review by Press Monitor covers the most impactful developments tracked by print media monitoring across Indian newspapers.

1. Delhi Launches Mega MSME Capacity Building Programme
“A front-page report in The Pioneer says” Chief Minister Rekha Gupta launched a Mega Capacity Building Programme for the city’s MSME sector on Thursday. The Chief Minister announced that the Centre has approved %49.74 crore for Delhi under the RAMP scheme to train over 3O,OOO small businesses and connect more than lO,OOO of them to digital markets by January 2O27. The programme, organised by the Delhi State Industrial and Infrastructure Development Corporation (DSIIDC) at Anuvrat Bhawan, was held under the Raising and Accelerating MSME Performance scheme. More than 2OO MSME entrepreneurs attended, along with Industries Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa and senior officials. The Chief Minister said the programme marked an important step toward what she called the “4-P Reform,” covering policy, process, performance and partnership. She said a partnership between Government and entrepreneurs could give fresh momentum to Delhi’s economy.  She said the RAMP scheme funding would help link over 3O,OOO MSMEs to modern skills and training, while more than lO,OOO businesses would be connected to digital platforms like GeM and ONDC to access larger markets. She said going digital was now essential for business competitiveness rather than optional. The Chief Minister said improved coordination between the Centre and the Delhi government was directly benefiting traders and entrepreneurs in the city.
Why it matters: Chief Minister Rekha Gupta launched a Rs 49.74 crore programme to train over 30,000 MSMEs and connect 10,000 to digital platforms under the RAMP scheme.
Key detail: The 4-P Reform – Policy, Process, Performance, Partnership – aims to boost Delhi's 2.48 lakh startups and 125 unicorns.

Source: The Pioneer (front-page), also covered by Millennium Post and Statesman.
Next step: Entrepreneurs in Delhi should explore training modules and GeM/ONDC onboarding.

2. NITI Aayog Pushes Early Skilling for Entrepreneurs
A front-page report in Mint says Niti Aayog has proposed integrating employability and entrepreneurship training from Class 6 and vocational tracks from Class 9. The think tank suggests making General Employability and Entrepreneurship Skills a separate subject for grades 11-12 and repositioning apprenticeships as a mainstream pathway.
Why it matters: NITI Aayog proposes employability and entrepreneurship training from Class 6 and vocational tracks from Class 9.
Key detail: General Employability and Entrepreneurship Skills as a separate subject for grades 11-12; apprenticeships as mainstream pathway.

Source: Mint (front-page), also covered by The Pioneer.
Next step: Education policymakers and SMBs should align apprenticeship programs.

3. AI Lowering Advertising Costs for Indian SMBs
A front-page report in Business Standard says 87 per cent of small and medium-sized businesses in India say AI-powered advertising tools have helped them access previously unreachable advertising channels. The report indicates that 75 per cent of Indian SMBs believe AI-enabled advertising has supported business growth, while 68 per cent say it has unlocked greater creativity.
Why it matters: 87% of SMBs say AI-powered tools unlocked previously unreachable advertising channels.
Key detail: 75% report business growth, 68% cite greater creativity.

Source: Business Standard (front-page).
Next step: SMB owners should evaluate AI advertising platforms for cost-effective reach.

4. Second-Gen Entrepreneurs Embrace Tech and Freedom
A front-page report in The Economic Times Family Business Dialogue in Bengaluru says second-generation entrepreneurs are shaping business choices through experience and freedom. Business leaders including Shruti Shibulal of Tamara Leisure, Viren Prasad Shetty of Narayana Health, Arun K Chittilappilly of Wonderla Holidays, and others discussed tech-driven expansion and patient capital.
Why it matters: Leaders like Shruti Shibulal and Viren Prasad Shetty discuss tech-driven expansion and patient capital.
Key detail: Family businesses in Bengaluru are leveraging technology and experience for growth.

Source: Economic Times (front-page).
Next step: Next-gen entrepreneurs can draw lessons on balancing tradition with innovation.

5. Govt Pushes Standardised Farm Financing for Contract Farming
“A front-page report in Mint says the government has asked public sector banks and the Indian Banks’ Association to develop a standard loan product and uniform documentation for contract farming, including financing for farm machinery, within 6-12 months. The proposed framework envisages an anchor buyer or processor tie-up, with buyer payments routed through an escrow account with a defined waterfall. It would include sub-limits for input finance, procurement advances, warehouse receipt finance and processing capex. Lending decisions would be based on the reliability of the buyer's purchase agreement, rather than collateral,” according to two sources. The government also proposed that the SEPEs in India, IBA and Nabard are referenced to explore Credit Guarantee Fund and Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises, National.
Why it matters: Standard loan product and uniform documentation for contract farming will ease credit access for small farmers and agri-SMEs.
Key detail: Lending based on buyer purchase agreement, not collateral; includes escrow account.

Source: Mint (front-page).
Next step: Agri-SMEs should prepare for simplified loan processes.

How Modi Managed “THE MEDIA” To Stay In Power

In 2002, Gujarat CM Narendra Modi sat in front of a BBC camera and admitted his one real weakness:
“One area where I was very, very weak… that was how to handle the media.”

He never forgot that lesson. He just decided the media should never be allowed to become a problem again.
Fast forward to 2026.
Between March and July, the government sent one blocking order every 68 seconds to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube.

1.95 lakh orders in five months.
1,275 every single day.
Instagram — the platform students used during the Jantar Mantar protests — received more than 1 lakh of them.
Last year the daily average was six.

This is not “managing” the media.
This is industrial-scale silencing.

The same playbook that started with ED and CBI cases against NDTV, the takeover of Network18, and UAPA against NewsClick’s founder is now running on autopilot through the Sahyog portal. Content vanishes in three hours. Often without anyone even seeing the order.

A government that needs to issue a takedown every 68 seconds is not confident.
It is terrified of what people will say when they are not being watched.

That is how you stay in power for this long — not by answering questions, but by making sure the questions never reach the public.

When dissent is treated as a security threat and protest as a crime, the media is no longer a watchdog. It is just another department to be controlled.
The 2002 admission was honest.

The 2026 response is the real story. 68 seconds.
That’s how long this government takes to silence you.
He admitted one weakness in 2002. He spent the next 24 years making sure it never happened again.

IFF’s Statement on the Blocking of X Account of the Cockroach Janta Party

22 May 2026

On May 21, 2026, the X (formerly Twitter) handle of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) (@CJP_2029) was withheld in India under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. IFF strongly condemns the blocking of the CJP’s X handle as a blatant misuse of State power and an arbitrary and disproportionate attempt to stifle freedom of speech and expression, a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India.

According to reporting by The Indian Express on May 22, 2026, the blocking directions were issued on the basis of inputs from the Intelligence Bureau citing threat to the sovereignty of India, jeopardizing national security and the fact that the account was gaining traction among young people. Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000, empowers the Central government to direct any Government agency or intermediary to block public access to information in the “interest of sovereignty and integrity of India, defence of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States or public order or for preventing incitement to the commission of any cognizable offence”. While Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 permits blocking on limited grounds, these grounds cannot be vague and speculative. Political commentary and criticism of public institutions are protected forms of speech under the Indian Constitution. The popularity of the account or the fact that the account mobilised young people through political expression cannot by itself be treated as a threat to national security.

The Indian Express’s report mentions that “blocking orders are issued under a confidential framework” which is deeply concerning. We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court of India upheld Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) on the basis that it is a narrowly drawn provision with several safeguards in place, including written reasoning for the blocking that is subject to legal challenge. State censorship like the blocking of CJP’s X account propagates opacity and provides affected users with no options for redressal, thereby effectively defeating these safeguards. IFF calls on the Union government to ensure timely notices are provided to affected users along with clear grounds and avenues for remedy.

IFF has previously explained how users whose constitutional rights are being infringed upon by the State can seek restoration of their blocked content. If you are an Indian social media user or journalist whose content has been blocked due to a government order, please write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in.
